title: Physical and Chemical Change
description: A physical change changes the size or shape of matter but not what it is made of. A chemical change creates a NEW substance with different properties.

exercises.question: Cutting a piece of paper is a ___ change.
exercises.exp: Cutting only changes the shape — paper is still paper. That is a physical change!

exercises.question: Burning wood is a ___ change.
exercises.exp: Burning creates ash and smoke — totally new substances! That is a chemical change.

exercises.question: Which is a PHYSICAL change?
exercises.exp: Melting ice is physical — water is still H₂O whether solid or liquid. No new substance is made.

exercises.question: Which is a CHEMICAL change?
exercises.exp: Sour milk has new substances formed by bacteria — that is a chemical change you can smell!

exercises.question: A physical change is usually ___.
exercises.exp: Most physical changes can be undone: melted ice can refreeze, torn paper can be taped!

exercises.question: When iron RUSTS, a new reddish substance forms. This is a ___.
exercises.exp: Rust is iron oxide — a brand-new substance. Rusting is a chemical change.

exercises.question: Mixing baking soda and vinegar makes bubbles and a new gas. This is a ___.
exercises.exp: When baking soda and vinegar react, carbon dioxide gas is produced — a new substance! Chemical change.

exercises.question: Tearing a piece of bread is a ___.
exercises.exp: Tearing only changes shape — the bread stays bread. Physical change!

exercises.question: Which SIGN tells you a chemical change happened?
choices: a new colour, smell, or gas appeared
exercises.exp: New colour, bubbles, smell, or light/heat are clues that a chemical change happened.

exercises.question: Baking a cake is a ___ change because ___.
choices: chemical — a new substance is created that cannot be unbaked
exercises.exp: You cannot turn a baked cake back into raw batter — a chemical change created something new and permanent!

exercises.question: Ice cream melting is a ___.
exercises.exp: Melted ice cream is still ice cream — it just changed from solid to liquid. Physical change!

exercises.question: Which pair both shows CHEMICAL changes?
choices: tearing cloth and crushing a can
exercises.exp: Both burning (creates ash/smoke) and rusting (creates iron oxide) produce new substances — chemical changes!

exercises.question: Shaping clay into a pot is a ___ change.
exercises.exp: Shaping clay only changes its shape — the clay is still clay. You can reshape it again. Physical change!

exercises.question: Fireworks explode with bright colours and loud bangs. This is a ___ change.
exercises.exp: Fireworks produce light, sound, heat, and new gases — all signs of a chemical change!

exercises.question: Which is the BEST clue that a chemical change occurred?
choices: the object changed colour permanently and produced a new smell
the object was cut in half
the object was heated but stayed the same
exercises.exp: Permanent colour change plus a new smell = new substances formed = chemical change!

exercises.question: Grapes are made into wine through fermentation. Is this physical or chemical?
choices: chemical — new substances like alcohol are produced
physical — you can turn wine back into grapes
exercises.exp: Fermentation is a chemical change — microorganisms convert grape sugars into alcohol and carbon dioxide.

exercises.question: A student folds aluminium foil into a boat shape. This is a ___ change.
exercises.exp: Folding only changes the shape of the aluminium — it is still aluminium. Physical and reversible!

exercises.question: Cooking meat on a barbeque turns it brown and gives it a new smell. This is ___.
choices: a chemical change — new substances form when meat is cooked
reversible if you cool it down
exercises.exp: Cooking meat causes chemical reactions — proteins denature and new flavour compounds form. Chemical change!

exercises.question: Which of these CAN be undone (reversed)?
exercises.exp: Frozen water can be thawed back to liquid — physical change! Burning, cooking, and rusting are permanent chemical changes.

exercises.question: Helium gas inside a balloon escapes when you open the valve. This is a ___ change.
exercises.exp: Releasing gas is physical — the helium molecules are unchanged, they just spread out into the air.

exercises.question: Which observation suggests a PHYSICAL change (not chemical)?
choices: the colour permanently changes to orange-red
a solid is broken into smaller solid pieces of the same material
exercises.exp: Breaking a solid into smaller pieces of the same material is physical — no new substance, just smaller pieces!

exercises.question: Leaves change colour in autumn. Scientists think this is partly chemical. What evidence supports this?
choices: new pigment colours (reds and oranges) appear as chlorophyll breaks down
exercises.exp: As chlorophyll (green pigment) breaks down chemically in autumn, other pigments like red and orange are revealed!

exercises.question: A snowman melts in spring. This is a ___.
choices: chemical change — snowmen cannot be rebuilt
physical change — water is still water whether solid or liquid
chemical change — melting creates a new substance
exercises.exp: Melting is a physical change of state — snow becomes liquid water but both are still H₂O. No new substance!

exercises.question: You mix yellow and blue paint together to get green paint. This is ___.
choices: a chemical change — green is a new substance
a physical change — no new substance is formed, pigments are just mixed
exercises.exp: Mixing paints is physical — the pigments blend together but no chemical reaction occurs. You could theoretically separate them!

exercises.question: Digesting food in your stomach is a ___ change.
choices: chemical change — enzymes break food into new smaller molecules
physical — the food just gets smaller
exercises.exp: Digestion involves chemical reactions — enzymes break down complex food molecules into simpler ones the body can use.

exercises.question: Which of these is an example of a REVERSIBLE physical change?
choices: water evaporating from a puddle (then condensing as rain)
exercises.exp: Water evaporation and condensation are reversible physical changes — water cycles between liquid and gas states.

exercises.question: A candle burns and gets shorter. Identify BOTH types of change happening.
choices: only physical — the candle gets smaller
both: wax melting (physical) AND wax burning/combustion (chemical)
exercises.exp: Two things happen when a candle burns: wax melts (physical) and wax vapour combusts with oxygen (chemical)!

exercises.question: Mixing sugar into water until it disappears is a ___.
choices: physical change — sugar dissolves but is still there
chemical change — a new sweet substance forms
exercises.exp: Dissolving is physical — sugar molecules spread through the water but no new substance is created. Evaporate the water and sugar returns!

exercises.question: Which change produces HEAT and LIGHT as evidence?
exercises.exp: Burning (combustion) produces heat and light — both are strong signs of a chemical change taking place!

exercises.question: A scientist wants to know if a change is chemical. She should look for ___.
choices: evidence of a new substance: colour change, gas, smell, or heat/light produced
exercises.exp: Scientists look for evidence of new substances — colour change, gas bubbles, new smell, heat, or light = chemical change.

exercises.question: Which statement about physical changes is TRUE?
choices: they change the appearance but not the composition of matter
they always produce heat and light
exercises.exp: Physical changes alter how matter looks (shape, size, state) but NOT what it is made of — same molecules, different form.

exercises.question: Toast is brown and crispy after heating. This is a ___.
choices: chemical change — new substances formed when bread was heated
exercises.exp: Toast cannot be un-toasted! Heat caused chemical reactions creating new substances (brown crust). Irreversible = chemical!

exercises.question: Which clue tells you that a CHEMICAL change happened?
choices: the object changed colour only because of paint
the object was cut in half
exercises.exp: A new smell means a new substance was created — that is evidence of a chemical change! (Like a match burning.)

exercises.question: Baking a cake involves mixing ingredients and heating them. The result is ___.
choices: a physical change — you can unmix the ingredients later
a chemical change — a new substance (cake) forms that cannot be turned back into raw ingredients
a physical change — only the colour changed
exercises.exp: Baking is a chemical change — eggs, flour, and sugar react with heat to form brand-new substances. No going back!

exercises.question: A metal bicycle left in the rain turns RUSTY. This is a ___.
choices: chemical change — iron reacts with oxygen and water to form iron oxide (rust)
exercises.exp: Rusting is a chemical change — iron reacts with oxygen and water to form a completely new substance: rust (iron oxide).

exercises.question: Which of these is a PHYSICAL change?
choices: crumpling a piece of aluminium foil
exercises.exp: Crumpling foil only changes shape — same aluminium, just bent. The other three produce new chemical substances!

exercises.question: Vinegar and baking soda produce bubbles when mixed. This is a ___.
choices: physical change — the substances just moved
chemical change — carbon dioxide gas (a new substance) was formed
exercises.exp: Bubbles of carbon dioxide gas — a brand new substance — prove a chemical change occurred!

exercises.question: A LOG OF WOOD burned in a fireplace leaves ash. Can you get the wood back?
choices: no — burning is a chemical change and the original wood is permanently gone
yes — add water to the ash
exercises.exp: Burning is an irreversible chemical change. The wood molecules broke apart and new substances (ash, CO₂, water vapour) formed.

exercises.question: You tear paper into tiny pieces. Which type of change is this?
choices: physical — it is still paper, just smaller pieces
chemical — you cannot re-attach the pieces
exercises.exp: Tearing only changes size and shape — the tiny pieces are still paper. This is a physical change!

exercises.question: Which evidence would NOT suggest a chemical change?
choices: an ice cube getting smaller in warm air
exercises.exp: An ice cube melting is a physical change — it is still H₂O, just liquid. The other three are signs of chemical changes.

exercises.question: Melting butter and cooking butter are DIFFERENT because ___.
choices: melting is chemical; cooking is physical
melting is physical (reversible, same substance); cooking is chemical (new substances form and it cannot be uncooked)
both are the same physical change
exercises.exp: Melted butter can re-solidify — it is the same fat molecules. Cooked butter undergoes chemical changes — you cannot un-cook it!

exercises.question: Concrete sets HARD after mixing water with cement powder. This is a ___.
choices: physical change — it just dried out
chemical change — water reacts with cement to form a new hard substance
reversible physical change — add water to soften it again
exercises.exp: Cement hardening is a chemical reaction — new calcium silicate crystals form. You cannot dissolve it back with water!

exercises.question: Which TWO are physical changes?
choices: cutting fruit and dissolving sugar in water
exercises.exp: Cutting fruit (just changes shape) and dissolving sugar (sugar still exists) are BOTH physical changes. No new substances!

exercises.question: Which is an example of a REVERSIBLE physical change?
exercises.exp: Melted chocolate hardens again when cooled — same substance, same composition. A perfectly reversible physical change!

exercises.question: Fireworks produce bright colours, light, heat, and smoke. This is a ___.
choices: physical change — colours are just paint
chemical change — chemical reactions release energy and form new substances
exercises.exp: Fireworks are dramatic chemical changes — gunpowder reacts to release energy (light, heat) and new gases form explosively!

exercises.question: Why is DIGESTION a chemical change?
choices: digestive juices and enzymes break food into completely new molecules the body can absorb
exercises.exp: Digestion uses enzymes to chemically break food into completely new, smaller molecules (sugars, amino acids, etc.). Chemical!

exercises.question: You mix food colouring into water. The water turns blue. This is a ___.
choices: chemical change — a new substance formed
physical change — food colouring dissolved but no new substance was made
chemical change — the colour proves a reaction
exercises.exp: Dissolving food colouring is physical — you could filter or evaporate the water to recover the dye. Same substances throughout.

exercises.question: Which is the BEST definition of a chemical change?
choices: any change where matter gets smaller
a change where new substances with different properties are formed
any change to the shape of an object
exercises.exp: A chemical change produces new substances with new properties — like rust, ash, or gas. That is the key definition.

exercises.question: Leaves change colour in autumn. Is this a physical or chemical change?
choices: chemical — the green chlorophyll breaks down and new pigments appear, changing colour permanently
physical — leaves can turn green again instantly
exercises.exp: Autumn colour change is chemical — chlorophyll breaks down and yellow/red pigments (always there, just hidden) become visible!

exercises.question: Which is most likely to be IRREVERSIBLE?
exercises.exp: Burning a candle is a chemical change and mostly irreversible — wax is consumed, CO₂ and water vapour escape. The others are reversible physical changes.

exercises.question: An egg is cracked open and fried. The white turns from clear to white. This is ___.
choices: chemical — proteins in the egg white react with heat and permanently change structure
reversible — cool the egg to make it raw again
physical — you can unfry an egg
exercises.exp: Heat permanently unfolds and re-links egg proteins (denaturation). Fried eggs cannot become raw eggs — irreversible chemical change!
